title: Advanced Micro Devices Earnings Beat as Data Center Revenue Nearly Doubles
excerpt: Record revenue of $13.38 billion rose 45% and adjusted EPS jumped 74% to $2.09 as Data Center sales hit $8.55 billion, and AMD guided fourth-quarter revenue to about $17 billion.
body:
• Advanced Micro Devices posted record third-quarter revenue of $13.38 billion, up 45% year over year, with non-GAAP earnings of $2.09 per share, up 74% and ahead of the $1.94 Zacks Consensus Estimate.
  • Data Center revenue nearly doubled, rising 97% to a record $8.55 billion — 64% of total sales — on demand for EPYC server processors and the launch of Instinct MI450 accelerators.
  • GAAP earnings of $1.46 per share trailed the adjusted figure mainly because of a $1.1 billion non-cash charge from revaluing warrants issued to customers.
  • What to watch: AMD guided fourth-quarter revenue to about $17 billion, plus or minus 3% — roughly 66% growth — and on its earnings call projected company revenue growth of more than 80% in 2027, according to Zacks.

Advanced Micro Devices posted record results on November 3, as its data center business approached two-thirds of total sales. The Santa Clara chipmaker reported third-quarter revenue of $13.38 billion, up 45% from a year earlier and above the high end of its own guidance. Non-GAAP earnings rose 74% to $2.09 per share, beating the Zacks Consensus Estimate of $1.94, and revenue also surpassed the consensus Zacks compiled. GAAP net income rose 95% to $2.43 billion, or $1.46 per share.

"We delivered a record quarter with revenue exceeding the high end of our guidance as Data Center segment sales nearly doubled year-over-year."

— Dr. Lisa Su, AMD Chair and CEO

Su said demand for Instinct accelerators and EPYC processors continued to strengthen, and that growth should accelerate in the fourth quarter as AMD scales production of its Helios rack-scale systems and next-generation "Venice" server processors. Chief financial officer Jean Hu pointed to operating leverage: revenue grew 45% while non-GAAP earnings per share grew 74%. Non-GAAP gross margin was 56%, up two points from a year earlier, and non-GAAP operating income rose 75% to $3.92 billion, a 29% margin.

Data Center is now the company

Data Center segment revenue was a record $8.55 billion, up 97% year over year, driven by EPYC processor demand and the launch of the Instinct MI450 Series GPUs, the company said. The segment now accounts for 64% of AMD's revenue, up from 47% a year ago, according to Zacks' analysis of the results. AMD said customers including Anthropic, Meta, Microsoft, OpenAI and Oracle Cloud Infrastructure are running workloads on the first Helios rack-scale systems, which pair MI450 GPUs with sixth-generation EPYC CPUs.

The rest of the business was mixed. Client and Gaming revenue fell 8% to $3.7 billion: client revenue rose 7% to $2.9 billion on Ryzen mobile processor sales, while gaming revenue dropped 40% to $773 million on lower semi-custom and graphics sales. Embedded segment revenue was $1.1 billion. The split underlines how completely AMD's results now turn on AI infrastructure spending rather than the PC market.

Why GAAP and adjusted earnings differ

The $0.63 gap between GAAP earnings of $1.46 and non-GAAP earnings of $2.09 is mostly one non-cash item: a $1.1 billion charge, worth $0.66 per share, from remeasuring the fair value of warrants AMD has issued to certain customers, which moves with AMD's share price. Stock-based compensation and amortization of acquisition-related intangibles account for most of the rest. GAAP operating income still rose 123% to $2.83 billion.

Guidance raises the bar for the fourth quarter

For the fourth quarter of 2026, AMD expects revenue of approximately $17 billion, plus or minus 3% — growth of about 66% year over year and 27% sequentially at the midpoint — with non-GAAP gross margin of about 55%, a point below the third quarter's 56%. On the earnings call, according to Zacks, management projected revenue growth of more than 80% in 2027 and expected full-year 2026 Data Center revenue to more than double from 2025. That guidance is now the number to judge: the fourth-quarter report will show whether the Helios and Venice ramps can deliver the steepest sequential jump in the company's history.
